source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Identify the individual closest to the event and assign direct blame, because personal fault is the main target of a root cause analysis after a sentinel event.","B":"Document the event for legal purposes without changing care processes, because root cause analysis is separate from efforts to prevent recurrence.","C":"Determine whether the event can be removed from internal reports, because the main goal is to reduce the number of documented sentinel events.","D":"Identify underlying system and process factors that contributed to the event and develop actions to reduce the risk of a similar event recurring in the future."}}
source_row.rationale: Root cause analysis is intended to understand the system and process factors that contributed to a serious event and to guide changes that reduce recurrence. Option D reflects the Joint Commission's current sentinel-event expectations. Option A centers the process on personal blame rather than contributing factors. Option B separates analysis from preventive improvement. Option C treats the process as a reporting-reduction exercise rather than a patient-safety investigation.
source_row.source_detail: The Joint Commission — Sentinel Event FAQs: organizations should identify sentinel events, examine root causes and contributing factors, and make improvements/actions to mitigate risk of recurrence rather than focus the analysis on individual blame. Current Joint Commission sentinel-event guidance in 2026; page and current expectations rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: prioritization, continuity, confidentiality, quality/cost-effective care, legal/ethical rights and assignment/delegation activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
